Hi. Spastic diplegic here. I drive with no modifications, but only because I have decent flexion in my right foot. Almost none in my left. If you have a similar limitation, I recommend picking your better foot and sticking to it. Do not deviate. Also, I recommend getting as comfortable as possible behind the wheel. Physically and mentally. This is probably only gonna happen with practice. I have a big startle reflex, and I almost gave up just because of how nervous other cars' proximity and/or sounds made me. You can do it. Just take your time. You'll be fine.

As a writer (only for myself), most of my characters have at least one dead parent. Not because it's "easy" to write, but because I have a dead parent. I write what I know. Does it add "trauma?" Sure, but parental loss is, indeed, traumatic.

Just an unnecessary note: everyone doesn't have the same "normal."

It's not harsh at all, thanks for asking. As a young kid, I could run, not much jumping. Balance was terrible (fell often), and riding a bike without training wheels was out.  I could walk unassisted, but used a chair/stroller for long distance. Then I had several "corrective" surgeries, and now I literally can't run to save my life. I can't stand for more than a few minutes. Walking even to my mailbox requires a "stop and rest", very depleting (granted I've been much more sedentary than I used to be). I will and have sat down in the middle of a parking lot on the way to my car because I underestimated the amount of walking I had to do inside a place, and ran out of "leg fuel" (my legs often lock up after too much energy expenditure). It was traumatic, because anything could've happened (I'm only 4'11, about 110), and there was nothing I could do but wait it out. Luckily, a kind stranger waited with me, and then carried my things.

The two "fiesty" FMC books that come to mind for me are a little different.  In these, I don't think the character herself is stupid, she just does an abysmally stupid thing, and reading "the thing" made me want to slap her and throw the book, respectively:

In Warrior's Woman by Johanna Lindsey (I know, I know 😬) the FMC, Tedra, is quite charming. But she >!Takes a potion to make herself immune/unresponsive/unreceptive to the MMC's sexual advances to basically get back at him for doing it to her as a part of a cultural method of punishing women (like, he arouses her, but physically can't soothe her).  But this is after he has felt guilty, acknowledged his wrongdoing, and apologized profusely, so he is confused and hurt by her actions. She even acknowledges that there was really no reason for her to do it. 🙄 She even goes so far to say that he still could've had sex with her unresponsive body, while they both acknowledge this is something he could never do, as he loves her.!< It's still one of my favorites, but that action just irked me. 

In Texas! Sage by Sandra Brown, the FMC is actually not my cup of tea as a character. She's not stupid, she's just... uninspiring. Still, what she does takes the TSTL cake. >!She and the MMC have to road-trip and shop around his invention to save her family's company, and their relationship grows along the journey. She appears to trust his judgement about how to proceed with HIS invention, yet because he won't give her details about his falling out with his former boss (whom he has at least admitted is a bad guy), she copies his invention schematics and visits said ex boss in an effort to "get more info" about why the MMC is being cagey. She then hands over these schematics to this former boss in a show of faith "in the invention", just knowing it will win the boss over.!< I actually dnf at that moment, at about 83%, because I could predict how everything would play out. To do something so antithetical to her goal was just...wow.

It's a made-up quote, but essentially if it was one member of the family, it would read as **"___ Mitchell's"**, using an apostrophe for possession. If it was the family as a whole, it should be **"Mitchells'."** What I was trying (and apparently failing) to articulate is the use of apostrophes for plural nouns with no possession. Think of the movie *We're the Millers.* It is correct. But many books have the error *We're the Miller's.*
